content:
The biggest advances have been in inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid, psoriatic and axial spondyloarthritis. Biologic medicines, cheaper biosimilar versions and JAK inhibitor tablets now give many people good control. For osteoarthritis there is still no medicine that reverses joint damage, so exercise and weight management remain the main treatments. Research is active, and you can volunteer for UK trials.

Inflammatory arthritis: more options than ever

Biologics. These target specific parts of the immune system. They include anti-TNF medicines and others that block IL-6, IL-17, IL-23 or B cells. Most are given by injection or infusion. On the NHS, NICE sets the criteria for when they can be offered, usually after standard DMARDs have not worked well enough.

Biosimilars. When a biologic's patent ends, near-identical versions called biosimilars can be made. They work in the same way and have made treatment more affordable for the NHS, so more people can access it. You may be switched to a biosimilar. Ask your team if you have questions.

JAK inhibitors. These are tablets that block signals inside immune cells. They are an option in rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis. Safety advice from the MHRA means they may be used with caution in people over 65, smokers and those at higher risk of heart disease, clots or cancer.

Treat to target. Not a drug, but a big shift: teams now measure disease activity regularly and adjust treatment until it is controlled. This approach helps many people reach remission.

Osteoarthritis: what is new and what is not

Osteoarthritis research is looking at medicines that might protect cartilage, injections of various kinds, and better ways to target pain. So far none of these is recommended by NICE as a routine treatment. NICE (NG226) does not recommend hyaluronic acid injections, and it does not recommend glucosamine or other supplements.

What does help, according to NICE, is:

  • regular, tailored exercise, often through structured programmes such as ESCAPE-pain
  • weight loss if needed
  • topical anti-inflammatory gels for knee and hand osteoarthritis
  • joint replacement surgery when other treatments have not helped and symptoms are severe

Newer weight-loss medicines may help some people with osteoarthritis indirectly by reducing weight. They are available on the NHS only under specific criteria.

Be cautious with "breakthrough" claims

Stem cell injections, platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and similar treatments are widely advertised privately. NICE has not recommended them for routine use in arthritis, and they can be expensive. Before paying, ask:

  • What does NICE or my specialist say about it?
  • What are the risks and the full cost?
  • Is this part of a registered research study?

Taking part in research

Clinical trials are how new treatments are proven. In the UK you can search for studies on the NIHR's Be Part of Research website and register your interest. Your rheumatology team may also tell you about trials. Taking part is voluntary, and you can withdraw at any time.

Talk to your team

If your current treatment is not controlling your symptoms, ask your GP or rheumatology team what other options there are. Treatment changes are common, and new options keep arriving.

Questions worth asking at your next review

  • Is my arthritis as well controlled as it could be?
  • Are there other medicines I would be eligible for if this one stops working?
  • Are there any research studies I could take part in?
  • Is a biosimilar version of my medicine available?

Treatment for inflammatory arthritis is personal. What works well for one person may not suit another, so it is normal to try more than one option before finding the right one. Keep a note of your symptoms and side effects between appointments to help your team decide.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
